strengths: Elegant and practical system design: the camera uses only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor, preserving nearly all incident photons (no coded apertures or filters), which is a genuine advantage over CASSI-like and filter-based systems in photon-limited regimes.

Fast, physically interpretable reconstruction: the plug-and-play ADMM with eigenspace projection and a BCCB-based fast matrix inversion achieves sub-second reconstruction (0.64 s), a meaningful engineering contribution that distinguishes the work from slow FISTA-style solvers (e.g., SDC at >15 min).

A real hardware prototype was built and demonstrated, with calibrated PSFs (Fig. 2b), real captures of lab scenes, a Macbeth chart evaluation with SAM and ΔE00 metrics, and robustness studies vs. distance and number of measurements (Fig. 5). Code and data are stated to be publicly available, supporting reproducibility.

The comparison methodology attempts fairness: matched 5-second total exposure across modalities, Poisson photon noise simulation, and accounting for transmission/absorption of optical components, and the paper honestly reports where it is not best (second place in SAM, performance degradation >600 nm, ΔE00 of 3.77 above perceptual threshold).

Limitations are candidly discussed (depth range dependence, paraxial field of view, >3 measurements required, static scenes), and the metameric real/fake food example (Fig. 3, points 5-6) is a compelling demonstration of reduced hallucination versus data-driven baselines.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination undermines the headline SOTA claim: the low-rank prior P is built from eigenvectors of the Harvard dataset [6] (via [2]), yet the main quantitative benchmark (Table 1) is '30 images from the Harvard dataset.' The claimed PSNR/SSIM advantage over KRISM (24.10 vs 21.12 dB) may partly reflect prior familiarity with the evaluation data rather than a better sensing modality. Evaluation on held-out spectra would substantially strengthen the claim.

Most quantitative comparisons are simulated, not measured: baselines (MST, Choi et al., KRISM, SDC, TF) are simulated by the authors under their own assumptions about noise, exposure, and optical effects, and real-data evaluation is limited to a Macbeth chart and a few staged lab scenes at a fixed 2.8 m distance with center-cropping. The center-cropping to the paraxial region sidesteps lateral chromatic aberration and spherical-aberation-induced focal shifts, so the effective field of view on real data is much smaller than the 10° FoV reported in Table 1.

Conceptual novelty is incremental: spectral focal sweep via chromatic aberration is well established (Cossairt & Nayar [10], Huang et al. [17], Zhan et al. [31], Zhao et al. [32]), and the algorithmic core (plug-and-play ADMM [8], spectral low-rank projection, off-the-shelf denoiser [18]) is standard. The contribution is largely the specific combination, the OTS-lens implementation, and the BCCB fast inversion formula, which is more of a well-executed engineering advance than a new principle.

The 'no hallucination / interpretable' argument is only partially supported: the pipeline still uses a learned denoiser and a learned spectral subspace, so data-driven components remain; the hallucination claim is backed qualitatively by one pepper example rather than a systematic study.

Practical operating envelope is narrow: static scenes only, a 34 cm depth of field around 2.8 m, targets on the optical axis, a 5-12 measurement mechanical lens sweep, and the 'high frame rate' in Fig. 1a relies on a simulated 5 s total exposure, which conflates exposure-limited frame rate with acquisition rate for a multi-shot sweep.

Real-data quantitative results are mixed: average ΔE00 of 3.77 exceeds the perceptual threshold of 2, SAM degrades for wavelengths >600 nm due to low illuminance, and the model assumes constant magnification across the sweep and ignores defocus within the depth of field — assumptions whose error budget is deferred to the supplement rather than quantified in the main paper.

strengths: The proposed system is a genuine hardware realization: a two-lens off-the-shelf prototype with measured PSFs (Fig. 2b) spanning 400–694 nm, which lends credibility to the claims of optical simplicity and photon efficiency.

The physics-based plug-and-play ADMM algorithm with a low-rank spectral projection and a BCCB-based fast matrix inversion is technically sound and achieves sub-second reconstruction (0.64 s), a meaningful improvement over the >15 min runtimes of comparable optimization-based systems (Table 1).

The paper reports the best PSNR (24.10 dB) and SSIM (0.61) among compared methods under a shared photon-budget simulation protocol, with careful accounting of per-modality transmission/absorption effects and exposure times.

Simulated comparisons include the metameric real/fake food example (Fig. 3, points 5–6), which is a compelling demonstration of the material-discrimination value of the method relative to data-driven baselines like MST.
Robustness analyses on real data (Fig. 5) — varying distance from the calibration plane and number of measurements — address practical deployment concerns beyond a single operating point.
weaknesses: Real-world validation is thin: the only quantitative real experiment is a Macbeth color chart at a single distance, under controlled illumination, with targets deliberately confined to a narrow 34 cm depth-of-field and a center-cropped paraxial region (Sec. 4.3). Average ΔE00 of 3.77 is actually above the perceptual threshold of 2, which weakens the color-accuracy claim rather than supporting it.

Several model assumptions are acknowledged but not empirically resolved: lateral chromatic aberration and spherical-aberration-induced focal variation are unmodeled and handled by cropping to the image center, severely restricting the effective field of view (10° FoV, but effectively much smaller in practice).

The simulation protocol embeds assumptions that favor the proposed method: ideal camera (no quantization, no readout noise, negligible transition time), static scenes, and a fixed 5 s total exposure regardless of number of exposures. The system requires a mechanically translated lens over multiple frames, so real transition/actuation times are not reported, making the '<1 second' end-to-end claim dependent on an idealized capture model.

Novelty relative to prior spectral focal-sweep work ([17], [31], [10]) is incremental: the encoding idea (exploiting chromatic focal shift with simple lenses) is established; the main contribution is the regularized plug-and-play inversion, and the algorithm relies on an off-the-shelf deep denoiser trained on hyperspectral data [18], which sits uneasily with the paper's emphasis on 'interpretable, physics-based' reconstruction and its criticism of data-driven hallucination.

Only five simulated test images (Fig. 3) are shown qualitatively, and Table 1 aggregates 30 Harvard images under one brightness condition; there is no ablation of the choice of eigenspace dimension v, denoiser, or measurement count in the simulated SOTA comparison, and no error bars or variance reporting.

The stated limitation that the method needs >3 (up to 10) measurements undermines the 'fast' narrative for dynamic scenes; all claims are confined to static, well-illuminated, depth-constrained targets, which substantially narrows the practical impact relative to the introduction's motivating applications (e.g., dynamic or low-light scenes).

Presentation issues: minor typographical errors ('on there publicly available datasets', 'the algorithm used in [31] is an naive inverse filtering'), and key details (ADMM derivation, fast inversion formula, optics, transmission modeling) are deferred entirely to the supplement, making the main paper insufficient for reproducing the method from the manuscript alone, though the authors state code and data will be released.

strengths: Complete system contribution: the paper presents a full computational imaging pipeline — optical design (two off-the-shelf lenses with naturally occurring chromatic aberration), measured PSF calibration (Fig. 2b), a physics-based plug-and-play ADMM reconstruction, and a working hardware prototype with real captures — rather than a simulation-only study.

The reconstruction algorithm includes task-specific, technically substantive contributions: eigenspace spectral projection (low-rank prior) and a fast BCCB-based matrix inversion that enables sub-second (0.64 s) reconstruction of a large hyperspectral inverse problem, addressing a real weakness of prior optimization-based CASSI-like solvers.

Comparison protocol is unusually careful for fairness: equal total exposure (5 s) across modalities, simulated Poisson photon noise, and accounting for optical blocking/absorption effects per modality — many prior comparisons neglect these. The proposed method achieves the best PSNR (24.10 dB) and SSIM (0.61) and second-best SAM among compared systems (Table 1, Fig. 3).

Real-data validation goes beyond qualitative pictures: quantitative Macbeth color chart evaluation with SAM and CIE Delta-E00, robustness sweeps over distance from the calibration plane and number of measurements (Fig. 5), and demonstrated metameric discrimination between real and fake food items (Fig. 3, points 5/6), which supports the claimed spectral accuracy advantage over data-driven methods.

Practical appeal is strong: light-efficient (no light-blocking elements), compact (4 optical components vs. up to 20 for KRISM), built from catalog parts, with code and data promised on GitHub — good reproducibility potential.

Limitations are candidly discussed (restricted depth range, paraxial FoV, >3 measurements needed for RGB, static scenes), and mitigation strategies are reported (center-cropping, positioning targets near the optical axis).
weaknesses: The quantitative SOTA comparison (Table 1) is entirely simulation-based; real-data quantitative results are limited to a Macbeth chart under a single low-light condition (25 lux), so the claimed superiority over MST/KRISM/Choi et al. is not directly verified on real captures of those systems.

Model mismatch is acknowledged but not fully characterized: unmodeled spherical aberration, lateral chromatic aberration, and defocus are handled by restricting the scene (center-crop, targets within a 34 cm depth of field at 2.8 m). This makes the practical imaging volume quite small, and the generalization beyond the calibration plane is shown only as a 30 cm robustness sweep on a planar target.

Real-data spectral accuracy is imperfect: SAM degrades for wavelengths > 600 nm due to low SNR, and the average Delta-E00 of 3.77 exceeds the perceptual-equivalence threshold of 2. The paper argues these differences 'go unnoticed in practice,' but this claim is not supported by user study or additional evidence.

Fairness of the simulation comparison depends on simulated implementations of competing systems; several assumptions (ideal camera, zero readout noise, no quantization, negligible transition time) may favor or disfavor specific baselines in ways that are hard to audit, and details are deferred to the supplement.

The method requires N sequential measurements with a mechanically translated lens, so despite the light efficiency argument, it is not demonstrated on dynamic scenes; the conclusion admits this. The frame-rate advantage in Fig. 1a relies on a simulated 5 s exposure rather than a demonstrated fast capture.

The spatial resolution gain relative to the blurry measurements relies on the denoiser prior; the hallucination claim ('minimal hallucination artifacts') is supported by qualitative patch comparisons only (yellow pepper example), not by a dedicated quantitative artifact or spectral-fidelity analysis.

Some methodological details needed for independent reproduction are deferred to the supplement (ADMM derivation, fast inversion formula, optical simulation details, noise model per modality), so the main paper alone is not self-contained.

strengths: Simple, practical optical design: the system uses only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor, exploiting natural longitudinal chromatic aberration rather than custom DOE/coded apertures. This is a meaningful hardware simplification over competing systems with up to 20 optical elements, and the prototype is fully calibrated with measured PSFs (Fig. 2b).

Strong empirical evidence: the method is compared against 8 baselines spanning different modalities (tunable filters, CASSI variants, DOE, spectral defocus) under matched total photon budgets, achieving best PSNR/SSIM and near-best SAM (30.81 dB / 0.92 / 7.35°) in simulation, and consistent real-data performance (29.54 dB on Macbeth patches). The low-exposure experiment (Fig. 3b) convincingly demonstrates robustness advantages of photon-efficient optics plus physics-based reconstruction.

Well-engineered inverse algorithm: plug-and-play ADMM with a low-rank spectral eigenspace projection and a derived BCCB-based fast matrix inversion yields sub-second (0.64 s) reconstruction, an interpretable alternative to purely data-driven methods with demonstrated stability under Poisson noise.

Honest self-assessment: the paper clearly states limitations (working depth range of 34 cm, degraded red/black recovery, multi-shot requirement, need for further noise modeling), and quantifies robustness beyond the theoretical working range (Fig. 5b). Code and data are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.

Clear writing and a well-motivated narrative connecting photon efficiency, optical simplicity, and reconstruction robustness, supported by qualitative failure analysis (e.g., pinwheel 700 nm failure case, spectral oversmoothing from the low-rank prior).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core sensing idea: reconstructing spectra from chromatically defocused focal stacks has been explored by He et al. [21], Zhan et al. [54], and the focal-sweep literature (Cossairt & Nayar [13], Huang et al. [26]). The main contributions are the robust reconstruction algorithm and system engineering; the paper should more explicitly delineate its algorithmic novelty relative to these prior chromatic-focal-stack approaches.

Multi-shot mechanical scanning undermines the 'fast imaging' claim for dynamic scenes: five images require translating a lens on a linear stage, so the method is restricted to static scenes within a narrow 34 cm depth range at ~2.8 m. This is acknowledged, but it substantially limits practical usefulness relative to snapshot CASSI-style systems, and the comparison in Table 1 could better foreground this acquisition-time/scene-motion constraint.

Comparison fairness concerns: MST [7] is a deep network trained for a specific CASSI forward model, and evaluating it under a different simulated modality/illumination may disadvantage it (the paper itself notes MST's 'narrower spectral coverage due to training/calibration data'). Some Table 1 entries also appear questionable (e.g., Tunable Filter PSNR of 4.78 dB, KRISM compute time of 0 s), warranting clarification of simulation protocols.

The low-rank eigenspace prior P is derived from the Harvard dataset, which conflicts somewhat with the paper's criticism of data-driven hallucination; dependence of results on this basis (e.g., spectral oversmoothing, metamer handling) is only briefly addressed.

Writing quality issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('PNSR', 'apried', 'witha robust reconstruction algorithm enables, for stable performance'), and key details (eigenvalue count v, µ1/µ2 settings, noise models, magnification-constancy assumption) are deferred to the supplement, making the main paper insufficient for full verification of the claims.

The assumption that magnification remains constant across the focal stack, and the paraxial/narrow-FOV regime (9.7° cropped), restrict real-world applicability; the depth-of-field and working-range limitations mean the system requires careful scene setup.

strengths: The paper presents a complete computational imaging system: a simple, well-motivated optical design (two off-the-shelf lenses exploiting longitudinal chromatic aberration), a calibrated physical forward model using measured PSFs across 29 spectral bands, and a fast inverse algorithm (plug-and-play ADMM with a low-rank spectral prior and BCCB-based fast inversion achieving sub-second runtime).

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: comparisons against eight systems spanning four encoding modalities (spectral filters, dispersers, DOEs, chromatic aberration) under equalized photon budgets and exposure times, across three public datasets, plus a real hardware prototype validated against LCTF ground truth (29.54 dB PSNR / 7.42 deg SAM on a Macbeth color checker, consistent with the 30.81 dB / 7.35 deg simulation numbers).

The robustness analysis is valuable and honest: measurements-vs-performance ablation (Fig. 5a), depth-of-field sensitivity (Fig. 5b), low-exposure behavior (Fig. 3b), and clearly stated failure cases (700 nm pinwheel channel, black regions, long-wavelength focal shift flattening).

Strong practicality: photon-efficient optics (no light-blocking elements), sub-second reconstruction, off-the-shelf components, and code/data release. The claim that a 4-component system outperforms systems with up to 20 elements is well supported by Table 1.

The physics-based iterative reconstruction with a data-driven denoiser is a sensible hybrid that plausibly mitigates hallucination of purely end-to-end methods, and the paper provides evidence of MST's low-exposure hallucination to support this narrative.
weaknesses: The system requires N=5 sequential measurements via a mechanically translated lens, so it is not snapshot; the authors acknowledge that dynamic scenes remain open. The 'fast' framing (sub-second reconstruction) should not be conflated with fast capture, and a 5-second total exposure in the main benchmark is generous.

The comparison experiments simulate all competing hardware systems using the authors' own implementations and calibration assumptions (illumination, quantum efficiency, light transmission per element). While photon budgets are equalized, small differences in simulation fidelity could favor the proposed modality; real captured results are shown only for SfD, not for the baselines.

Restrictive operating assumptions: a narrow paraxial FOV (9.7 deg crop), a 34 cm depth working range at ~2.8 m, and constant magnification across the focal stack. The paper shows robustness slightly beyond the predicted range, but these limits constrain practical deployment and are only partially explored in the supplement.

The low-rank spectral prior (eigenvectors from the Harvard dataset, following [1]) can oversmooth spectra, as the authors note; the dependency on the prior dataset's statistics and the choice of eigenspace dimension v are not ablated in the main text.

Several presentation defects suggest insufficient proofreading: 'PNSR' (Sec. 4.2), 'apried' (Conclusion), the garbled sentence 'addresses shot noise witha robust reconstruction algorithm enables, for stable performance' (Sec. 4.2), and inconsistent figure notation. These are correctable but detract from clarity.
Table 1 reports 0 s compute time for KRISM and 0 s for the tunable filter without clear definition of what is included, which could mislead readers comparing computational costs.

strengths: The core contribution is compelling: a chromatic focal sweep camera built from only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor, achieving state-of-the-art simulated reconstruction quality (Tab. 1: best PSNR 30.81 dB and tied-best SSIM, second-best SAM) with sub-second reconstruction (0.64 s) — a strong practicality/quality trade-off versus systems with 9–20 optical elements.

Both simulation and real hardware are provided: a physical prototype with measured PSFs (Fig. 2b), calibration via LCTF-scanned point source across 29 bands, and real-data results validated against LCTF ground truth (Fig. 4a) and Macbeth patches (Fig. 4b, 29.54 dB / 7.42 deg, closely matching simulation). This end-to-end demonstration materially strengthens the credibility of the claims.

The comparison methodology is unusually careful: equal total exposure time and photon budget across modalities, Poisson noise and light-efficiency modeling, and baselines spanning four optical modalities and three reconstruction families (Tab. 1, Sec. 4.1).

The algorithm contains real technical substance beyond off-the-shelf components: eigenspace projection exploiting low-rank natural spectra, a modified plug-and-play ADMM (Eq. 3, Alg. 1), and a BCCB-based fast matrix inversion enabling sub-second runtimes despite large convolutional operators (Sec. 3.2, 4).

Robustness is analyzed rather than merely asserted: low-exposure results (Fig. 3b) show a clear advantage over data-driven methods that hallucinate (e.g., MST pepper failure), and depth robustness beyond the nominal 34 cm working range is quantified (Fig. 5b, artifacts only appearing ~29 cm beyond theoretical range).

Honest limitations section (Sec. 5) addressing working depth range, degraded red/black recovery, multi-shot requirement, and dynamic scenes, plus stated code/data release on GitHub supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Comparisons to competing systems rest largely on the authors' own simulations of those systems (with simulated PSFs, noise, and component efficiencies), so fairness depends on assumptions detailed in the supplement that cannot be fully verified from the main paper; e.g., KRISM's reported compute time of 0 and MST's settings could advantage SfD in the runtime column of Tab. 1.

The system is fundamentally multi-shot (5 translated lens positions), requiring a static scene and a mechanical sweep; the paper acknowledges dynamic scenes as future work, which significantly limits the 'fast imaging' framing relative to true snapshot methods.

The scene depth must fall within a narrow 34 cm working range (2.64–2.98 m) and the FoV is paraxial (9.7 deg crop from the sensor), which restricts practical use cases; evaluation scenes are all placed at a fixed 2.8 m, so real-world diversity is limited (four scenes plus a color checker in Fig. 4).

Some claims of superiority over the data-driven baseline MST rest partly on its low-exposure hallucination (Fig. 3b), but MST was trained on different spectral data than what it is applied to here — a potentially biased comparison the paper does not deeply discuss.

Reconstructed spectra are acknowledged to be oversmoothed by the low-rank prior (Sec. 4.2), and long-wavelength/black-region failures are visible (Fig. 4a, 700 nm pinwheel), meaning spectral fidelity is not uniformly strong.

Presentation issues remain: several typos/grammatical errors ('PNSR', 'apried with reconstruction algorithms', 'addresses shot noise witha robust reconstruction algorithm enables'), and some key details (PSF calibration protocol, BCCB derivation, mu1/mu2 settings, working range analysis) are deferred entirely to the supplement, making the main paper difficult to fully assess on its own.
